item.title: Choosing a Linux distribution is choosing what you will give up
item.description: Every Linux distribution is a set of decisions about who will sit at the machine, so choosing one means deciding which trade-offs you are willing to live with.
item.content:encoded:
A distribution is a set of decisions someone else made about who would be sitting at the machine. Choosing one means choosing which of those decisions to inherit, so the useful question is less “which is best?” than “what am I willing to give up?”

Newest and proven pull against each other

Software that has just been released has, by definition, spent the least time in other people’s hands. A system that ships the newest versions gives up the long record of use that a system built for reliability leans on, and the reverse holds too. If one system were both the newest and the most proven, there would be nothing to choose. In practice Fedora and Arch are the names people reach for when they want the latest software, while Debian and CentOS are the usual picks for a server that must stay stable.

Effort against control

Ubuntu and Linux Mint are friendly to newcomers and well documented, which makes them the sensible first system. Arch sits at the other pole: every part of the system is yours to steer, and the price is that you must already understand a good deal, or learn it fast. Picture the difference between heating a ready meal and cooking from raw ingredients. The first is on the table in minutes and teaches you little. The second teaches you what a meal is made of, and the early attempts are worse.

Who answers when it breaks

Red Hat Enterprise Linux and SUSE Linux Enterprise Server carry formal certification and support aimed at businesses, and both are common where companies run servers and cloud infrastructure. That matters to a person as well as a machine: if the goal is a career in enterprise IT or cloud administration, learning the Red Hat family is an advantage.

The family name hides where a system sits

Lineage and position are different things. Fedora, CentOS and RHEL belong to one family, the one associated with enterprise use and reliability. Yet Fedora is the answer for someone who wants the newest software, CentOS for a stable server, and RHEL for a business that needs backing. One household, three answers to the same questions. Treat the family as a first guess about where a system sits, then check the particular member.

One choice, traced to the end

Start with a question that comes before the others: will anyone click around on this machine? Desktop editions arrive with a graphical interface, such as GNOME, KDE or XFCE, and everyday applications already installed. Server editions are a different kind of system. Now run a case, someone who wants to work in cloud administration and has no need for a screen.

goal             work in cloud administration
screen needed?   no                 -> a server edition
newest software? no                 -> proven over fresh
backing needed?  yes                -> Red Hat or SUSE family
shortlist        RHEL, SLES
cost             the newest software, most likely

The last line is the one worth saying aloud. A choice that cannot name its cost is unfinished. The beginner’s case shows why that is hard: when you cannot yet say what you would give up, take the system that asks the least of you at the start, because a well-documented one leaves your questions with answers waiting.

What this leaves unsettled

These three trades are my own sorting, and they overlap. A system may be easy partly because it is stable, which would make effort and freshness less independent than they look. The trace also treats a person as fixed, though someone who starts on Ubuntu can want more control a year later. Does what they learned carry over toward Arch, or does it have to be rebuilt? And is the family label ever more than a useful guess for someone still choosing, as opposed to someone already inside one?

item.title: Multiplying Without a Times Table: The Neighbor Trick
item.description: Every digit of a product can be built from just a digit and the one beside it, and that small idea unlocks a whole system of mental arithmetic.
item.content:encoded:
Jakow Trachtenberg was a Ukrainian-Jewish mathematician and engineer who ended up a prisoner in a German Nazi concentration camp. To keep his mind occupied, he built a system of rapid mental calculation: a set of small, memorizable operations for multiplying, dividing and adding quickly. The 1960 book that later presented his method describes seven years in various camps, with most of the work done without pen or paper.

Its pitch is a strange one: multiplication without multiplication tables. How could that possibly work?

Let’s start with the easiest case and find out.

Start with eleven

Take 342534253425 and multiply it by 111111. Don’t reach for the standard method. Ask instead what multiplying by 111111 actually means.

11x=10x+x11x = 10x + x11x=10x+x

Multiplying by ten slides every digit one place to the left. Adding xxx back in means that each place in the answer receives two digits: the digit that was already there, and the digit that slid in from its right.

So every digit of the answer is a digit plus its neighbor, where “neighbor” means the digit immediately to its right. Put a zero in front of the number and a zero behind it, so that the ends have neighbors too, and the work looks like this:

Digit Its neighbor Sum
0 3 3
3 4 7
4 2 6
2 5 7
5 0 5

Read down the last column and you get 3425×11=376753425 \times 11 = 376753425×11=37675. No times table was involved, only addition. When a sum passes nine, you write the units digit and carry the extra to the next place on the left.

Notice the direction, too. You work from right to left, producing the answer one digit at a time, and each digit needs only a glance at two neighbors.

Why does twelve work the same way?

Run the same argument again, now with 121212.

12x=10x+2x12x = 10x + 2x12x=10x+2x

The 10x10x10x part again hands each place the digit from its right. The 2x2x2x part adds double the digit that is already there. So the rule is: double each digit, then add its neighbor.

Try it on 316316316, with a zero written in front. Working from the right:

Digit Double + neighbor Carry in Write Carry out
6 12+012 + 012+0 0 2 1
1 2+62 + 62+6 1 9 0
3 6+16 + 16+1 0 7 0
0 0+30 + 30+3 0 3 0

That gives 316×12=3792316 \times 12 = 3792316×12=3792.

Both rules came from splitting the multiplier into a ten plus something simple. Keep that in mind, because it carries almost everything that follows.

The strange one: five

What is the equivalent trick for 555? Here it helps to notice that 555 is half of ten:

5x=10x25x = \dfrac{10x}{2}5x=210x​

Halving is a digit-by-digit operation too. Multiplying by ten slides the digits left, and halving then pulls half of each digit down into place. The result is again a rule about neighbors:

  • Take half of the digit’s neighbor, rounding down.
  • Add 555 if the digit itself is odd.

Why the 555? Because an odd digit has half a unit left over when you halve it, and that half spills into the place beside it as a 555. The system’s own phrasing is that the 555 makes up for the 0.50.50.5 dropped in the next digit’s calculation.

Trachtenberg wanted this halving to be instant. Nobody should think “half of seven is three and a half, so three.” You should think “seven, three,” and move on.

Check it on 93×593 \times 593×5:

Digit Half of neighbor Odd bonus Result
3 0 (trailing zero) +5 5
9 1 (half of 3) +5 6
0 (leading) 4 (half of 9) none 4

Read upward and you get 465465465.

Why can we build six and seven from five?

We have already seen the pattern, so the next step is to split the multiplier again.

6x=5x+x6x = 5x + x6x=5x+x and 7x=5x+2x7x = 5x + 2x7x=5x+2x

For six, take the five-rule and add the digit itself. For seven, take the five-rule and add double the digit. So the rule for six is: add half of the neighbor to each digit, plus 555 if the digit is odd. The rule for seven is: double each digit, add half of the neighbor, plus 555 if the digit is odd.

Here is 357×6357 \times 6357×6, from the right:

Digit Sum Write Carry
7 7+0+5=127 + 0 + 5 = 127+0+5=12 2 1
5 5+3+5+1=145 + 3 + 5 + 1 = 145+3+5+1=14 4 1
3 3+2+5+1=113 + 2 + 5 + 1 = 113+2+5+1=11 1 1
0 0+1+1=20 + 1 + 1 = 20+1+1=2 2 0

That gives 214221422142. And 693×7693 \times 7693×7 works the same way:

Digit Sum Write Carry
3 6+0+5+0=116 + 0 + 5 + 0 = 116+0+5+0=11 1 1
9 18+1+5+1=2518 + 1 + 5 + 1 = 2518+1+5+1=25 5 2
6 12+4+0+2=1812 + 4 + 0 + 2 = 1812+4+0+2=18 8 1
0 0+3+0+1=40 + 3 + 0 + 1 = 40+3+0+1=4 4 0

The answer is 485148514851.

Notice what is missing: no row recalls a product from a table. Everything is doubling, halving, adding, carrying and one tiny neighbor lookup.

The ones that use subtraction

A few of the rules flip the idea around, using complements instead. For 999, you subtract the rightmost digit from 101010, subtract each remaining digit from 999, and add the neighbor. For the leading zero, you subtract 111 from the neighbor.

Try 2130×92130 \times 92130×9:

Digit Calculation Write Carry
0 (10−0)+0=10(10 - 0) + 0 = 10(10−0)+0=10 0 1
3 (9−3)+0+1=7(9 - 3) + 0 + 1 = 7(9−3)+0+1=7 7 0
1 (9−1)+3=11(9 - 1) + 3 = 11(9−1)+3=11 1 1
2 (9−2)+1+1=9(9 - 2) + 1 + 1 = 9(9−2)+1+1=9 9 0
0 (leading) 2−1=12 - 1 = 12−1=1 1 0

The result is 191701917019170. Eight, four and three have their own variants of the same shape, and the digit-by-digit habit never changes.

What if both numbers are big?

So far the multiplier has been a single digit. For two long numbers, Trachtenberg’s general method keeps the same one-place-at-a-time spirit.

Think about the last digit of the product. It is settled entirely by the last digits of the two numbers, so it can be written down at once. The next digit to the left depends on that temporary result plus two cross products: last digit against next-to-last, and next-to-last against last. Then you write that digit and carry.

Each place in the answer sums everything that can reach it:

the sum, over all pairs of digits whose positions land on that place, of the products of those digits, plus any carry

His version splits every small product into a units digit and a tens digit, which land in neighboring places. He called it the 2 Finger Method. With practice, people can multiply four-digit numbers in their heads, writing down only the final answer, starting at the right and ending at the left.

Division follows the same one-digit-at-a-time shape, but with subtraction in place of addition. You work out the answer digit by digit, subtracting products from a running partial dividend. If a subtraction goes negative, you back up one digit and reduce that answer digit by one.

What the trick really is

Look back at everything above. A big multiplication was never treated as one scary operation. Each answer digit was treated as a small, local question: what do I need from here, and from the digit beside me?

That is what made it usable for someone without paper. The memory load stays small, because the problem arrives in tiny pieces and the answer leaves in order, right to left.

And it all started from the plainest observation: 11=10+111 = 10 + 111=10+1.

item.title: About
item.description: Otmane Echaibi, systems hacker, minimalist, writer, amateur mathematician and marathon runner.
item.content:encoded:
I’m Otmane Echaibi, a systems hacker. I live in the terminal, and my home is the internet.

I write Python, Fish, Lua, Go, Rust and JavaScript. Each one has one job, and Python sits in the middle:

Outside the terminal I run marathons, write, and do math as an amateur.

I’m a minimalist, and it’s my philosophy, not a style. I keep my things few and my code small. The blog follows the same rule: say what’s needed, then stop.

What you’ll find here

Notes on how things work: systems, code, math, and what long-distance running teaches about both. Math starts from the simplest case and builds up. I would rather leave something out than pad it.

Say hello

Corrections, questions and arguments are welcome on the contact page.

item.title: Contact
item.content:encoded:
Found a mistake? Have a question, a topic request, or just want to talk math and code? I’d love to hear from you.

Reach me

  • Email: sudotoo@protonmail.com
  • GitLab: https://gitlab.com/alephlam

Corrections

I do my best to get every fact right. If you spot an error in a post, please tell me which post and which line, and I’ll fix it and credit you if you’d like.

Response time

I’m a one-person blog with a day job, so replies can take a few days. I read everything.

item.title: Privacy Policy
item.description: What this blog does and does not collect.
item.content:encoded:
Last updated: September 2026

The short version

This blog does not use analytics, advertising, tracking cookies, or comment systems, and it does not ask you to create an account. There is very little to say here, on purpose.

What happens when you visit

This site is a set of static pages served by GitLab Pages. When you load a page, your browser requests files directly from GitLab’s infrastructure, which, like any web host, logs standard technical data (such as IP address, browser type, and requested URL) for operation and security. I do not receive, store, or use that data myself. See GitLab’s privacy statement for how they handle it.

  • No first-party cookies are set by this site.
  • No third-party trackers, ad networks, or social-media pixels are embedded.
  • The search page runs entirely in your browser against an index built when the site is generated. Your search terms never leave your device.
  • The light/dark theme choice is remembered using your browser’s local storage, on your device only.

If this changes

If I ever add privacy-respecting, cookie-less analytics, I will update this page first.

Links to other sites

Posts may link to outside sources. Once you click through, that site’s own privacy policy applies.

Contact

Questions about this policy? See the contact page.
